method: A = 3+ knowledge bases or a won debate, and fits our style. B = fits and needs no missing data. C = needs a missing feature or data feed. D = style conflict. Keyword and scope heuristics; research input only.
note: Advisory only. Nothing here changes live order engines. Hard gates need an owner pick.

rules.title: Be selective; not trading is valid
rules.rule: Take only a few high-quality setups, avoid overtrading, and accept no-trade days; knowing when not to trade preserves capital.

sources.statement: Assess the regime first and trade only when the picture is clear to you; if evidence is missing, wait or walk away.
Be highly selective: take directional bets only when all factors align, roughly once or twice per quarter at most.
Not trading is as important as trading; knowing when to wait is a discretionary edge.
Prioritize capital preservation; knowing when not to trade matters as much as knowing when to trade.
If your validated strategy gives no trade today, do not trade; a no-trade day beats a rule-breaking loss.
Swing trade 2-3 times per week, holding positions for days to weeks.
The more you learn, the less you trade; fewer trades earn more.
You do not have to trade every day; trade only when the market fits your setups and skills.

rules.title: Dealer gamma regime: mean-revert vs trend
rules.rule: In positive gamma, fade moves and trade reversion between gamma levels; in negative gamma, expect amplified trending moves and trade with momentum.

sources.statement: Paid source: statement withheld.
When dealers are short gamma and put hedges are being bought back, expect a trend day and hold the move.
Use dealer gamma regime to gauge chop: strongly negative total gamma means directional sessions; positive gamma means consolidation; reduce futures size and favor mean reversion in choppy periods.
Positive net gamma implies a mean-reversion regime; negative net gamma implies a trend-following regime — use it as a first filter.
Before any trade, determine whether price is above or below zero gamma; above = mean-reverting, below = trending.
Positive gamma exposure: dealers buy dips and sell rips (mean-reverting); negative gamma: dealers chase moves, better to hold runners.
[Fredy Sarmiento] In positive gamma, trade mean reversion: price runs to a gamma level and reverses toward the next one.
In a negative-gamma environment dealers hedge by selling futures into declines, amplifying moves; read the regime from net 0DTE gamma.

rules.title: Define exits and risk before entry
rules.rule: Before every trade, define and record the max loss, stop, targets and position size, and confirm the account can absorb the loss.

sources.statement: Pre-define and label exit points — stop loss and targets — for every trade; the rest of a trading system is noise.
Before every trade, define what you trade, why, when, from which level to which target, and the risk.
Start every trade by asking max downside first, then upside.
Before every trade answer: how much am I willing to risk, what is my profit target, and at what point will I exit if wrong; otherwise you are gambling.
Define both the profit exit and the loss exit before entering any trade.
Paid source: statement withheld.
Every option trade needs a journaled entry reason and exit plan because time decay pushes options toward zero.
Plan targets and quantities per exit before entry; keep stop quantity synchronized with the remaining position as targets fill.

rules.title: Enter on retest of broken level
rules.rule: After a level or value edge breaks, enter on the pullback or retest of that level, with targets at the next level.

sources.statement: Enter longs on the first pullback to VWAP after a qualified break above it.
On Fed days, enter only after a 5-minute close outside the pre-Fed range and a confirming retest, once the press conference is over.
If the session opens outside prior value, expect price discovery: wait for a test of the value edge with sellers exhausting and buyers taking control, then go with it.
When price gains a level, enter on the retest of that level and target the next level up.
Favorite setup: after a trend and small range, draw a P-shaped profile; on a higher high, buy the retest of its VAH when sellers are absorbed and buyers push with result; stop below.
Short setups: wait for a sustained break below support followed by a pullback.
Plan trades fully: after a breakout from the zone, enter the pullback with a limit order.
[Fabio Valentini] After an initial-balance breakout, look to enter on the retrace into the zone between the breakout value area edge and the POC, where buyers are expected to reload.

rules.title: Scale out at first target, protect runner
rules.rule: Take partial profits (often ~50%) at the first target, move the stop on the remainder to breakeven, and let a runner work.

sources.statement: Paid source: statement withheld.
Scale out: first target then move stop to breakeven, second target at session highs.
Use multiple targets: take ~50% at the first target and leave a runner.
Manage in stages: as a trade moves favorably, raise the stop to cut risk; then move the stop to entry ('free ride'); then take partial profits and trail the remainder.
Paid source: statement withheld.
When an option doubles, sell enough contracts to recover the original cost and hold the remainder at no net risk.
Pay yourself along the way by scaling out into the move instead of holding for the whole move.
When a long-term holding rallies hard, sell about half to take your initial capital out and let the rest ride risk-free.

rules.title: Wait for reaction at the level
rules.rule: A level, zone or gamma wall is not an entry by itself; wait for price to reach it and react or reclaim with confirmation before entering.

sources.statement: Do not place blind limit orders on plain support-as-support (range) touches; wait for confirmation there.
A gamma wall alone is not a trade; price must come to the level first and the approach decides the entry.
At key levels, wait for order-flow evidence (reclaim after overshoot, opposing pressure drying up) before entering; the same evidence governs exits.

[World Class Edge, speaker unattributed] Don't place a limit order as soon as price reaches the zone; watch the reaction and enter with the stop above the reversal top for tighter risk and bigger size.
Do not trade a fair value gap on sight; require more confluences and an idea beyond the gap itself.
An attractive reference zone (e.g., log regression band) is not sufficient for entry; wait for price and timing targets.
A call wall does not mean price touches it and reverses forever; it is where options positioning concentrates.
On a slow approach watch for a direct reaction at the level; on a fast approach let price overshoot and enter only on the reclaim.

rules.title: Don't let emotions drive trades
rules.rule: Follow your plan objectively and do not let fear, greed, FOMO or the need to be right drive trading decisions.

sources.statement: Acknowledge your fear, look at it, and take the planned trade anyway; do not let greed or fear drive decisions.
Before every trade ask why you are entering; a racing heart means over-risking and trading on hope means overtrading.
Most traders lose not from lack of skill but lack of emotional control; fear, greed, revenge trading and impulsivity cause losses.
Do not let fear or greed drive in-trade decisions; closing or adding is fine only when not emotionally motivated.
Follow a plan rather than emotions; emotional traders panic sell downturns and panic buy tops.
Stay objective and follow a systematic process during disruption.
Do not chase FOMO; there is always another week.
Do not get emotionally attached to a stock or a coin.

rules.title: Fade failed breaks that reclaim
rules.rule: When price pokes beyond a level or value edge, fails to hold and reclaims it, fade back toward the other side of value.

sources.statement: Enter on a failed auction: price pokes below value, aggressive sellers are absorbed by passive buyers, then buyers take control; target the other side of value.
A wick beyond a level that fails to close past it is a failure; expect price to reverse toward the next level in the opposite direction.
Safest variant: trade the pullback or break back into the prior value area.
Fade a failed downside break when price reclaims the reference after selling volume fails to make progress; abandon if price accepts below.

[World Class Edge, speaker unattributed] In a balanced regime, if price breaks below the value area low and closes back above it, expect a full rotation through the POC toward the value area high (~80% rule).
When shorting into resistance, wait for price to break above and fail back below before entering.
Read a daily candle that wicks outside the prior range and closes back within it as a bearish signal for the next day (mirror it for bullish).
If price breaks below the value-area low of balance and then closes back above it, expect a full rotation to the value-area high (~80% probability).

rules.title: Exit when traded level is invalidated
rules.rule: Exit immediately when price accepts through the level or structure that justified the trade, rather than waiting for the full stop.

sources.statement: Exit immediately if price loses the confirmed pullback low or closes back below the reclaimed level.
If price fails to bounce from the level you entered on and loses it, exit at break-even.
If price crosses the liquidity level you traded against and continues, the analysis was wrong: exit.
A candle close beyond the value area low (acceptance) invalidates the long setup; exit immediately rather than waiting for the stop.
For cup-and-handle trades, enter only on a neckline break; a later break below the handle low signals a failed breakout — exit.
If price breaks a wall with strength and keeps accepting beyond it, stop fading it and reassess the map.
[Fabio Valentini] Treat acceptance back through the value area low (after a long IB breakout) as the invalidation point; exit there instead of waiting for the full range.
Exit a Fed-day breakout trade when the broken level is reclaimed.

rules.title: No martingale or revenge trading
rules.rule: Never increase size or re-enter to win back losses; after a loss, stick to the plan or stop.

sources.statement: Do not place a trade to win back a loss; if you would not make it otherwise, wait.
Never double risk after losses (martingale); a losing streak means the strategy is out of regime — stop.
Do not try to recover a stop with the next trade; chasing losses leads to sizing up and destructive revenge trading.
After a loss, stop for the session if you are chasing, revenge trading, doubling size, moving the stop or forcing setups.
After a loss keep the same goal and do not try to win it back with revenge trades; sell when you are up.
Do not re-enter to recover money after a session-loss trigger; require a reset and renewed evidence first.
[Fabio Valentini] Never double risk (martingale) after losses when the strategy is underperforming; stick to the plan and review.
Average down only on long-term investments, never on swing trades or day trades.

rules.title: Volatility-scaled stops and targets
rules.rule: Size stop width, and targets, to current volatility (ATR multiples, IV, VIX) and regime rather than using fixed points.

sources.statement: Size stops and targets by ATR so they scale with volatility instead of fixed ticks or percent.
Most systematic strategies collapse with tight stops because their edge cannot absorb random oscillation; test stop amplitudes.
Institutional reward-to-risk is not fixed but linked to instrument volatility and market regime.
Size stops to the day's volatility: a 30-point ES stop is huge at VIX 12 and noise at VIX 30.
Use looser stops in high volatility and tighter stops in low volatility.
Feature-study baseline exits used 1.5 ATR take-profit and 1 ATR stop-loss.
Default pullback system exits: target 4.5x ATR, stop 2.5x ATR.
Avoid tiny fixed intraday stops (e.g., 0.3%); intraday is erratic, so size stops to volatility.

rules.title: Breakouts need acceptance
rules.rule: Treat a breakout as valid only when price shows acceptance and progress beyond the level; failed or unaccepted breakouts imply rotation back into range.

sources.statement: Qualify a breakout only after a new range (acceptance) forms outside prior day's value; price discovery alone is not acceptance.
If breakout concepts fail (stops hit and price re-enters), expect a larger balance game and switch to range trading.
Judge a breakout by price response (acceptance and immediate progress), not penetration alone; the retested boundary should act in its new role.
Treat balance as broken only when price closes or builds value (acceptance) beyond the prior balance extreme.
Exit a breakout long when price distributes or is accepted back into the range.
Define acceptance above value as a full candle with its low above prior VAH before going long.
If price does not break out of the value area, expect rotation within it and filling of unfair (thin) price levels.
In compressed, choppy ranges, treat breakouts as unreliable until participation and acceptance improve; a break without prompt follow-through keeps the range hypothesis.

rules.title: Keep strategies and tools simple
rules.rule: Prefer simple strategies and a few core tools, removing extra indicators and complexity as noise and fragility.

sources.statement: Keep charts simple: use basic support and resistance for entries and strikes; too many indicators are just noise.
Complexity is fragility: every added rule is another claim the future must match the past.
Use Market Profile and Volume Profile as the base; simplify and remove extra tools — more is not better.
[Matteo Conti] Keep strategies simple; complexity is fragility, and the best-performing strategies are simple and understandable.
Prefer simple theses; long multi-step theses are less likely to be right.
Keep the number of added filter rules to a minimum; extra rules improve the backtest but make it worse at predicting the future.
Complicated methods like Elliott Wave may work briefly but not for years; simplicity wins.
Focus on a select handful of Greeks/metrics: delta, beta, implied volatility, volume and open interest; ignore the rest as noise.

rules.title: Short strikes beyond support/resistance
rules.rule: Place short put or credit-spread strikes at or beyond a support/resistance level expected to hold.

sources.statement: Place short call-spread strikes at resistance points and make sure you are paid a fair price.
Set the short put strike just below a local support zone, use the next strike down for the long leg, and target short-strike deltas of about 0.1-0.2.
After earnings, while premium is still high, sell further OTM puts near support and buy lower puts to cap risk.
Place the short strike of a credit spread beyond the level expected to hold; work limit orders on combos rather than accepting the displayed price.
Place iron condor and credit spread short strikes at technical support and resistance, and keep them fixed.
Place bull put spread short strikes at support or about one standard deviation away.
Use chart support for put strikes and avoid selling puts right above major levels where breakdowns could send the stock lower.

rules.title: Trade only liquid instruments
rules.rule: Check volume, open interest and bid/ask spreads before trading, and avoid illiquid instruments with wide spreads.

sources.statement: Avoid exotic currencies; they are illiquid and extremely volatile, like penny stocks of forex.
Avoid markets lacking sufficient liquidity; the odds are against you there.
Check volume, OI, quote size and spread width before buying options; theoretical value doesn't ensure a fill.
Trade only options with open interest above about 1,000, good volume and a tight bid-ask spread, including at deeper strikes.
Avoid oversized, leveraged positions in small, illiquid names that cannot be sold when everyone runs for the door.
Check order-book depth before sending a large market order: a thin book lets it eat through levels and pay slippage.
When selling options require tight bid-ask spreads, open interest and volume.
Check liquidity before sizing big trades; thin morning liquidity (e.g. FDAX) can cause bad stop fills.

rules.title: VIX 20 as regime line
rules.rule: Treat VIX below 20 as calm or risk-on and above 20 as fear, chop or de-risking, with readings above roughly 30-35 as extreme.

sources.statement: Read VIX under about 20 as calm, 20 to 29 as choppy and 30 or more as panic.
Treat VIX 20 as the line of demarcation: below 20 the market is complacent; above 20 it enters the 'chop bucket'.
VIX below 20 means institutions can run risk-on and invest in equities; above 20 many must de-risk.
Read a VIX above 20 as a sign of fear.
Treat VIX above 20 but below about 30-35 as normal-elevated; above that the regime is extreme.
With VIX back below 20 after turbulence, treat markets as calmed.
When VIX goes above 20, expect choppy conditions (the 'chop bucket') and be cautious.

rules.title: Size by dollar risk / stop distance
rules.rule: Set contract count as the fixed dollar risk divided by the stop distance (plus costs), so every trade risks the same amount.

sources.statement: Set a fixed small risk budget, such as 0.25% of the portfolio, and size shares by the distance from entry to stop.
Fixed fractional sizing risks a constant percentage of capital and must be set ex ante.
Size every trade to account and predefined risk; control the dollar loss if the level fails.
Contracts = accepted dollar loss / (stop distance x contract value + fees + slippage allowance), rounded down; if one contract exceeds budget, use a smaller contract or skip.
[Matteo Conti] Size positions by stop distance so every trade risks the same dollar amount: fewer contracts on wide-range days, more on quiet days.
When taking a trade with a wider stop than usual, cut your size so you do not get scared out of the position.
Size a share position so hitting the stop loses at most 5% of the account.
Position size = total capital x risk percent (e.g., $1,000 x 2% = $20 risk), adjusted to stop distance.

rules.title: Require candle close beyond level
rules.rule: Confirm a level or pattern break only after a candle closes beyond the boundary, not on intraday wicks.

sources.statement: Paid source: statement withheld.
When a candle closes beyond a level (gains it), expect continuation to the next level.
Wait for a triangle/pattern breakout before acting; a hard break below pattern support invalidates the setup.
Confirm a bullish intraday breakout by waiting for a candle close above VWAP before buying.
Enter only on a strong break of structure confirmed by a candle close.
Wait for the 30-minute higher-timeframe candle to close before executing; do not enter on an unclosed candle.
For breakouts, mark daily support/resistance, then wait for new closes beyond the level on a 15-minute chart and check the left side for obstacles.
Paid source: statement withheld.

rules.title: Distrust optimizer best-fit parameters
rules.rule: Treat optimized parameters as curve-fit historical bests: prefer robust parameter regions and validate before trading.

sources.statement: Treat parameters found by optimizers as historical best fits, not a guaranteed profitable system.
Backtests are not reality; beware overfitting (over-optimization) when validating systems.
When optimizing, pick robust parameter areas where results stay strong when inputs change slightly, not the top net-profit result.
[Matteo Conti] Avoid overfitting: don't tune entry/exit timing parameters just because they give the best historical equity line (data snooping).
Distrust the best of many rules tried on the same history; data-mined patterns found even in noise do not repeat on new data.
Automated optimization involves curve fitting; validate before trading the result.
Worry about overfitting, data snooping and noise—those are the real institutional problems.
Correct for the number of strategies tested: about 5 in 100 no-edge strategies pass a 5% significance test by luck.

rules.title: Crowded positioning is vulnerable
rules.rule: Treat extreme one-sided or consensus positioning, long or short, as a crowded trade vulnerable to sharp reversals and squeezes.

sources.statement: Paid source: statement withheld.
Watch futures positioning (COT) for extremes and look to trade against them.
When the whole market holds the same consensus trade, a binary event can move price against strong fundamentals purely on liquidity and positioning.
Expect sell-the-news drops when a trade is crowded and everyone is long, even when the story is right.
Paid source: statement withheld.
Check positioning skew: when there are essentially no shorts in a contract (e.g. RBOB), the long side is crowded and vulnerable.
When all participants are long, expect exhausted buying and a painful reversal; when your trade becomes the consensus, look for a new exposure.
Watch for record leverage, crowded one-sided positioning and money rotating out as signs a trade is topping.

rules.title: Edges decay with popularity
rules.rule: Expect edges to decay as they become popular or markets become more efficient, and keep searching for new ones.

sources.statement: Edges decay once popular or scaled; viral strategies like ORB will likely degrade within years.
Avoid relying only on popular chart setups; the most widely used technical patterns carry the least edge and are easiest for algos to exploit.
Alpha decays; never disclose a working edge and keep searching for the next one.
Expect pricing differentials to shrink as markets become more efficient; edge requires scale, logistics and information.
Expect published edges to weaken after they become widely known, as the size effect did after its publication.
Simple support/resistance trading no longer works as before; market whipsaws levels until it stops you out.

rules.title: Judge performance risk-adjusted
rules.rule: Evaluate performance by risk-adjusted, durable returns relative to drawdown, not by raw P&L.

sources.statement: Judge skill by return per unit of risk, not by beating the S&P.
Judge a desk by risk-adjusted, durable returns, not raw P&L; a smaller clean P&L beats a large one hiding basis risk and uncollateralised credit.
Optimize for risk-adjusted return, not raw return; judge strategies by drawdown taken to produce the return.
Judge performance on risk-adjusted terms (Sharpe), not raw profit; 40% with 3% drawdown beats 150% with 45% drawdown.
Compare investments by excess return per unit of volatility (Sharpe ratio), not by raw return.
Treat profit as an outcome, not the mandate; chasing P&L above all else is the fastest way to blow up a desk.

rules.title: Add only on confirmation or reduced risk
rules.rule: Add to a position only on predefined confirmation, after moving the existing stop to breakeven or reassessing risk.

sources.statement: Paid source: statement withheld.
When adding to a winner, first trail the original position's stop to entry so risk is confined to the new add-on.
Assign only part of the risk budget to the initial entry and add units only on predefined confirmation, after reassessing stop and remaining loss capacity.
Add to positions as they keep proving you right.
On a drawdown day, scale in only after the stop on the existing position can be moved to zero risk.

rules.title: Aim for modest consistent returns
rules.rule: Target consistent modest returns instead of chasing big wins or making up lost time with speculation.

sources.statement: Do not try to make up for lost time with aggressive or speculative investing; shortcuts leave people further behind.
Target ~20% annual returns with consistency rather than outsized returns.
Aim for consistent modest monthly gains (~3%/month) instead of overnight riches; chasing huge wins is like buying a lottery ticket.
Do not chase the one big trade; aim for consistent gains.

rules.title: Define complete, objective rules
rules.rule: Specify entry, exit, sizing and execution objectively enough that another person could execute the plan.

sources.statement: A raw signal becomes a strategy only with explicit entry eligibility, order type, expiry, exits, sizing and authority.
Make the trading plan objectively definable so another person could execute it.
Every strategy has three components—entry, exit and position sizing; do not neglect exits and sizing.
Define each automated trade preset by entry criteria, stop loss, take profit, size, time window and asset, and ask the AI to trade when criteria are met, not right now.
Use objective, non-bendable rules (volume/market profile, fixed price-action rules) so analysis is replicable; discretionary trendlines are not.
Write your trading rules down and make each one measurable; 'it has to be a good trade' is not a rule.
Write a trading plan that fixes the risk per trade, the assets, the timeframes and the number of losses before you stop.

rules.title: Location over trigger
rules.rule: Prioritize trade location over entry technique: trade only at clear locations such as value edges and never in the middle of balance.

sources.statement: Do not trade the middle of the balance; trade outside the balance where breakouts give information.
Counter-trade only at a clear location (e.g. prior value area / VPOC rejection with selling tail); wait for the pullback to that location rather than entering fast.
[Imre Gams] Location matters more than entry technique: at the right location for rotational or trending trades, almost any entry technique works.
Location matters more than entry trigger: any entry method works at the right level (e.g., VAL with delta divergence).

rules.title: Major moving averages as trend filter
rules.rule: Use the 50/200-day moving averages as the trend reference, and take bullish positions only when price is above them.

sources.statement: Paid source: statement withheld.
Before writing a put credit spread, confirm the underlying is in a bullish trend or at least not in a falling trend.
Use the 200-day moving average as trend reference: below it, the primary downtrend stays intact.
In a bull market, buy breakouts of leading stocks above the 100/200-day MA and near the 5/10/20-day MA.
Treat the 50-day moving average crossing below the 200-day as a sell signal and crossing above as a buy signal.
Read index closes above the 50- and 100-day moving averages as fairly bullish; treat the 200-day as the last level holding.

rules.title: Position sizing is the core skill
rules.rule: Treat position sizing as the core of risk management; big losses come from oversizing.

sources.statement: Money management answers one question: how many contracts to enter on the next trade.
Big losses come only from risking too much or not exiting when you should; a disciplined loss is a good trade.
Size and capital management matter more than the strategy; write your own rules, check average position size against the account, and journal trades.
The real killer is not knowing how to size trades around even a simple strategy.

rules.title: Stop hunting is a myth
rules.rule: Ignore stop-hunting narratives in deep markets and focus on price, volume and hedging flows.

sources.statement: Market makers in regulated markets do not hunt your stop losses; institutions hunt microstructure inefficiencies.
Market makers are hedging option inventory in futures, not hunting stops; price follows liquidity along the path of least resistance.
Ignore stop-hunting stories in deep markets like S&P or crude; focus on what price, speed and volume show.
Stop hunting by big players is largely a myth; nobody but your broker knows where stops are.

rules.title: Stops slip; plan for it
rules.rule: Expect stop orders to fill with slippage or gap through, so do not treat the stop as your exact max loss.

sources.statement: Size positions for possible gaps and slippage beyond your intended stop.
Don't treat a stop-loss order as max downside; assume gaps can fill you anywhere and plan for 100% loss of premium or a position going to zero.
[Imre Gams] Futures stops can slip, so risk is never fully defined; use small position size with stops, and remember net short options carries undefined risk.
Be careful with stop-limit orders; they may not fill when price drops fast.
A stop loss is a stop order executed at market once triggered; if the level is emptied, expect at least one tick of slippage.
Remember futures stops can slip; only net-long options give mathematically defined risk, while net-short options carry undefined risk.

rules.title: Target next structural level
rules.rule: Set profit targets at the next mapped structural level, such as daily highs/lows, value-area edges or liquidity.

sources.statement: Take profits at (3) daily highs/lows, (2) value area highs/lows, (1) visible order-book liquidity; a single large persistent resting level likely causes reversal.
Set profit targets from market structure.
Target the next mapped level and scale out on the way when trading multiple contracts.
Derive target areas from balance and imbalance (profile structure) to produce sensible reward:risk.
Take profit at or just below resistance.
In range trades, take profit or partials at the opposite side of the range.
When long in a trend, target the previous day's high and place the stop at the recent low.

rules.title: Run uncorrelated strategies for all regimes
rules.rule: Run several uncorrelated strategies, such as trend-following and mean-reversion, so every environment is covered and no single strategy's slump is fatal.

sources.statement: Run at least two strategies: one trend-following (momentum) and one mean-reverting (counter-trend).
[Fabio Valentini] Diversify across uncorrelated edges so they offset each other across quarters.
Run diversified, uncorrelated strategies (e.g., breakout plus mean-reversion to fair value) because any single model can fail for months.
Hold value and momentum together, since the two have tended to move in opposite directions and the mix is smoother than either alone.
Instead of modeling the regime, hold strategies for uptrend, downtrend, low-vol and high-vol environments.
[Matteo Conti] Hold at least three strategy families: trend-following, mean-reverting, and tail protection for sudden crashes.
Run several uncorrelated strategies across instruments; one strategy cannot make money all the time.

rules.title: Trim after overbought rallies
rules.rule: After large overbought run-ups, trim or protect leveraged and extended positions and expect a pullback or consolidation.

sources.statement: When a position nears its target in overbought conditions, take partial profits or raise the stop instead of leaving gains fully exposed.
Exit leveraged ETF positions after big rallies because volatility decay plus margin interest flips the risk/reward, even if long-term bullish.
Scale out or trim when the chart looks exhausted or extremely overbought, even if the trend and the earnings are intact.
When S&P 500 RSI reaches extreme readings (~77), expect a pullback; past breaches preceded 8-26% declines.
Trim leveraged positions when the market runs too hot and a pullback is likely; don't over-leverage.
Expect pullbacks after overbought conditions following a massive rally.
After an insane run-up, expect a stock to consolidate before its next leg up.

rules.title: Account for trading costs
rules.rule: Include commissions, spreads and slippage in research, since costs can exhaust small edges.

sources.statement: Include spreads, slippage and latency in research: NQ costs of 2-4 ticks can exhaust small gross edges such as fair-value-gap taps.
Require average trade above ~$80 per NQ mini contract to survive costs.
Watch commissions: dozens of small trades a day can cost more than the edge, especially with small competition accounts.
Include trading costs in every backtest, since leaving them out makes every rule look better than it is.
Keep commission below about 3% of the stop size; the tighter the stop, the more commissions eat the edge.
Mind costs: ten micro NQ cost about 2.5x the fees of one mini NQ.
Include commissions in every backtest.
Subtract taker and maker fees from a backtested edge; if scalping edges cannot clear the fees, move to hourly and longer trades.

rules.title: Avoid outright shorts
rules.rule: Avoid outright short positions, including SPX shorts, which carry poor hit rates or unlimited risk; express bearish views with capped-risk options instead.

sources.statement: Don't short the S&P outright; express bearish views with options because upward drift works against outright shorts.
Express a bearish sector or single-stock view with a bear put spread for defined risk.
Never short stock outright (unlimited downside); use poor man's covered puts instead.
Prefer the long side for anomaly trades because the zero floor caps downside; avoid shorting overvalued momentum names that can run indefinitely.
Do not buy puts or short the index as a strategy, since the market rises over the long run.
Outright SPX shorts had only a 31-35% hit rate in uptrends and ~42% in downtrends; buying won ~60% regardless of regime.

rules.title: Don't sell premium across earnings/news
rules.rule: Filter out premium-selling signals when jump risk such as earnings or major news is present, and sell premium in calmer periods instead.

sources.statement: IV-rich-vs-RV signals are false positives when jump risk (e.g., an upcoming earnings release) is present; filter them out.
Avoid selling puts right before earnings or big news events; sell during calmer periods instead of chasing high premiums.
Avoid 0DTE condors on major-news sessions.
Normally don't sell volatility (e.g., iron condors) across an upcoming earnings release.

rules.title: No tips; do your own research
rules.rule: Never trade on social-media tips or others' callouts; treat them only as a starting point for your own due diligence.

sources.statement: Never buy a stock just because someone told you to; do your own due diligence to build conviction to hold.
Never buy a stock based on a social-media tip.
Do not copy a large options order just because big money is behind it; check its timeframe, strike vs price, and catalyst.
Do your own due diligence instead of following financial YouTubers.
Never buy a stock only because it was going up; know why you own it.
Treat other people's callouts only as a starting point for research.

rules.title: Size inversely to volatility
rules.rule: Trade smaller in more volatile assets or stressed regimes, using volatility targeting.

sources.statement: A trade without position sizing isn't a trade; convert conviction and asset volatility into size (trade less of more volatile assets).
Reduce position size when VIX is elevated, for example above 27.
Adjust position size to the volatility of the instrument (volatility targeting) to improve risk-adjusted returns.
Check the VIX term structure; backwardation signals stress now, so adjust size.
Set market exposure to target volatility divided by forecast volatility, so size shrinks when forecast risk rises, and cap the exposure instead of borrowing above 100%.
Scale position size down when daily point ranges get very large, because typical sizing gets wrecked quickly.
Paid source: statement withheld.
Shrink positions when the GARCH volatility forecast rises, since high-volatility days arrive in clusters.

rules.title: Compression precedes big moves
rules.rule: Treat volatility or range compression as a precursor to a big move, and enter as price expands away.

sources.statement: Treat moving-average compression (20/50/200 clumped and flat after long sideways trade) as a precursor to a large move; enter as price pulls away from the averages.
Trade breakouts only when both price range and volume contract before expanding together.
Use a TTM Squeeze (volatility compression) for breakout timing and separate indicators (moving averages, custom RSI) for direction.
Very narrow intraday ranges and sub-17 VIX streaks signal consolidation before a big move.

rules.title: Define trend by swing structure
rules.rule: Define the trend by higher highs and higher lows (or the reverse) per timeframe, and treat it as intact while the defining swing holds with acceptance.

sources.statement: Treat a trend as intact while the defining higher low (or lower high) holds; a mere breach is insufficient without acceptance or an opposing swing sequence.
Classify each timeframe as one-time-framing up (higher highs, higher lows, higher closes), one-time-framing down (opposite), or balanced.
Favor stocks making higher highs and higher lows that continue the primary uptrend.
Define trend first via successive higher highs/higher lows (or lower lows/lower highs) before choosing a setup.

rules.title: Detect regime, deploy matching model
rules.rule: Explicitly detect the current regime, testing models live if needed, and deploy the strategy that fits it.

sources.statement: Detect the regime (compressing vs expanding) and deploy the model that fits it; a profitable trend model is wrong for compression.
Define regimes explicitly (quantified trend/volatility state) and test whether a regime filter (e.g., ADX for chop) actually helps the specific strategy.
[Fabio Valentini] In short competitions, run trend-following, mean-reverting and volatility-breakout models on separate accounts first to detect regime, then scale the one that fits.

rules.title: Exit long options well before expiry
rules.rule: Exit long options and debit spreads well before expiration (for example 10+ sessions or midweek for weeklies) to avoid accelerating theta.

sources.statement: Paid source: statement withheld.
Do not hold LEAPs to expiration; plan exits ahead of time because theta decay accelerates as expiration approaches, especially in sideways markets.
By Wednesday judge whether a weekly can still get in the money; OTM Friday contracts often fetch more midweek than at expiration.
Roll or sell a LEAP about three months before expiration, before theta decay ramps up, instead of holding it to expiry.
Avoid holding long options inside about 30-45 days to expiration, where extrinsic value decays quickly.

rules.title: Exit on fundamental thesis failure
rules.rule: Exit and accept the loss when fundamentals or physical supply/demand no longer support the position.

sources.statement: Hold a directional position without a price target as long as trend, supply, demand and data stay aligned; exit when they diverge.
Exit a LEAP when there is a fundamental shift in conviction, such as major news or financial issues that severely impact the company.
If the market isn't moving in line with physical supply and demand and you can't explain why, exit the position and accept the loss.
Exit a stock when the company stops delivering the products it promised.
Exit when the thesis breaks on a pre-written trigger, regardless of the price.
Reconsider a long-term holding mainly if the company starts losing money and becomes unprofitable.
Change your stance when circumstances change instead of staying glued to the same thesis; that is how you protect capital.

rules.title: Gamma walls as support/resistance
rules.rule: Treat the call wall and large positive gamma strikes as resistance/magnets and the put wall as support for intraday direction.

sources.statement: Treat the call wall (largest positive gamma strike) as the day's heaviest resistance and the put wall as the strongest support.
Large positive gamma strikes act as magnets and ceilings; rallies grind into them and stall.
Use 0DTE option flow levels (call wall, put wall) and the gamma regime to time intraday direction.

rules.title: Keep independent income while trading
rules.rule: Maintain a stable outside income so trading losses never threaten your livelihood.

sources.statement: Keep a stable income so survival does not depend on the portfolio; desperation increases mistakes.
Do not trade without independent cash flow; trading is not income replacement.
Never treat trading as your main source of income.
Keep a stable outside income while trading so a severe loss does not threaten your livelihood.

rules.title: Liquidity drives equities
rules.rule: Treat global and central-bank liquidity as the master driver, leading equities by months: injections support risk, withdrawal weighs on it.

sources.statement: Track the Fed balance sheet every Thursday when it is published, since risk assets suffer when the Fed withdraws support.
Treat liquidity as the master macro driver: liquidity injection supports equities, liquidity withdrawal/rate hikes produce prolonged grinding declines.
Treat liquidity and money supply as the main driver of stocks, ahead of earnings.
A QT halt and possible QE improve liquidity: lower yields, higher multiples, weaker dollar, supportive of Bitcoin and US stocks.
Global liquidity historically leads equity markets by about two to three months.

rules.title: Match method to your personality
rules.rule: Choose or adapt a trading style that fits your own character instead of copying someone else's.

sources.statement: Do not copy another trader's method; markets change and you must find a style suited to your own strengths that you enjoy.
Adapt the strategy to the trader's personality (Trader-DNA), not the trader to the strategy.
Choose a style matching your character; high-win-rate scalping does not suit everyone.

rules.title: Move stop to breakeven at trigger
rules.rule: Move the stop to breakeven once a defined trigger is hit, such as open profit equal to initial risk or price reaching a key gamma/call-wall level.

sources.statement: On IVB trades target ~1:2 to the statistically derived protection level; at a big positive-gamma level move stop to breakeven.
Once open profit equals initial risk (e.g. $500 risk, $500 open profit), move the stop to entry.
When price nears a call wall after your long, move the stop to breakeven.

rules.title: Process over single outcomes
rules.rule: Judge decisions by process across a large sample, not by single outcomes or streaks.

sources.statement: Judge yourself on the process, never on a single trade result.
Judge decisions by process, not outcome.
A winning streak is not evidence of edge; five heads in a row from a fair coin is ~3% and common across many attempts.
Judge decisions by process over a sample of ~100 similar trades, not single outcomes.
Score each trading day green only if every rule was followed, regardless of P&L, and tie a reward to a streak of green days.
Do not count wins that did not follow your edge as evidence that the edge is profitable.

rules.title: Reduce on major moving-average break
rules.rule: Reduce or reassess exposure when price breaks key trend moving averages (50/200-day or 50-week) or relative strength breaks.

sources.statement: Paid source: statement withheld.
When leading names lose their 10-day or 20-day moving averages and leading groups test higher-time-frame breakdown levels, treat market structure as changing.
Reduce crypto exposure after the first weekly close below the 50-week MA and again before a likely second close (to ~85% cash in the crypto sleeve).
Watch the 50-day moving average as support on mega caps; a break opens a move toward the 200-day.

rules.title: Rotate to trending, volatile markets
rules.rule: Choose or rotate into whichever market currently has strong volatility and a durable trend.

sources.statement: Rotate to whichever market is currently in a bull market or trending easily (e.g. oil during a geopolitical shock) when indices get hard.
Favor markets with large volatility and durable policy-driven trends (e.g. forex during major rate-cycle shifts) in top-down market selection.
[Jan Smolen] Rotate to whichever market currently has the volatility/bull market (e.g., oil, natural gas) rather than staying fixed on one asset.

rules.title: Verify claims before trusting
rules.rule: Examine the evidence for an idea and test it before trusting gurus or magic levels.

sources.statement: Run from gurus promising guaranteed easy income or 'never buy options, only sell'.
Before adopting an idea, examine the evidence, question assumptions, and learn where it has failed.
Do not trust advertised win rates; check whether break-even trades were discarded from the count.
Arbitrary magic retracement levels (e.g., ICT 79%) lack justification; test them before trusting.

rules.title: Very high win rates are unrealistic
rules.rule: Do not expect or trust very high win rates; they are not sustainable across market conditions.

sources.statement: Never expect to sustain a very high win rate; survive inevitable losers with risk control.
No genuine strategy has a 90% win rate; distrust anyone promising one.
Very high win rates are only achievable in specific market phases, not all conditions.
Treat a 90% to 100% backtest win rate as a sign of overfitting, not as proof of an edge.

rules.title: Sell only strikes you'd own
rules.rule: Sell cash-secured puts, put spreads and covered calls only on quality stocks at strikes where you would be happy to be assigned.

sources.statement: Sell cash-secured puts only at a strike where you actually want to own the shares, ideally well below the price for a cushion.
Sell cash-secured puts only on stocks you'd be willing to own at the strike.
Only sell cash-secured puts on stocks you actually want to own, at a strike price you would be happy buying at.
Sell cash-secured puts only on companies you are happy to own and could buy 100 shares of outright.
Don't pick a covered-call strike you'd resent being assigned at just because premium looks attractive.
Only write put credit spreads on blue-chip companies with strong fundamentals and technicals that you would hold in your own portfolio.

rules.title: Close-based stops, not single pierce
rules.rule: Trigger exits on closes beyond a structural level or indicator, not on a single intraday pierce.

sources.statement: On a 5-minute chart, three consecutive closes below VWAP plus a retest that holds means control has shifted; adjust the position. One stab through means nothing.
Back up a profit target with a trailing stop on the 9-period EMA of a 2-day chart; exit only on a close past the EMA, not an intraday pierce.
Exit momentum trades on a break and close beyond the prior bar high or low.
Paid source: statement withheld.

rules.title: Event IV builds then crushes
rules.rule: Expect implied volatility to build before CPI, FOMC, NFP and OPEX and to be crushed afterward, and factor the crush into event trades.

sources.statement: Incorporate the volatility-crush concept whenever trading through major scheduled events.
Expect IV to build before CPI, FOMC, NFP and OPEX and get crushed after.
Do not buy options as an earnings bet; implied volatility collapses after the report.
Around FOMC, CPI and NFP, expect an implied-volatility crush if price fails to move; put premium evaporates and supports upside.

rules.title: Expected move from IV/16
rules.rule: Estimate the daily expected move as IV (or VIX) divided by 16, scaled by the square root of trading days.

sources.statement: Read the VIX level as the implied one-year percentage range of the S&P 500, up or down.
Implied one-day move ≈ IV / 16 (square root of 1/252).
Expected daily move ≈ VIX ÷ 16 percent; mark it above and below the open.
Use one-week implied volatility to estimate the expected weekly range of a currency pair.
Expected move scales with the square root of time; use trading days (DTE x 0.69) rather than calendar days for precision.

rules.title: High-delta long-dated calls for stock replacement
rules.rule: Use deep ITM, roughly 95-delta, longer-dated calls for stock replacement and PMCC long legs.

sources.statement: Prefer longer-dated, high-delta calls for stock replacement because early daily decay is lower than weeklies/0DTE.
Replace core stock holdings with ~95-delta calls to free cash as dry powder.
Buy LEAPS deep in the money, between about 0.75 and 0.9 delta depending on liquidity.
For poor man's covered calls buy 95+ delta LEAPs, not 70 delta, to avoid a short-gamma / negative-delta trap.

rules.title: Hold core conservative allocation
rules.rule: Hold a core allocation to stable assets, sized by time horizon or age.

sources.statement: Always hold a core allocation to stability (cash, bonds to maturity, etc.).
Money needed within 10 years should be about 50% in conservative assets (bonds, cash); time horizon, not age, dictates risk.
Keep about 80% of the portfolio in long-term investments and trade only with a small portion.
Structure the portfolio into a safe base (cash, gold, bonds), a growth core (index plus quality names) and a capped high-risk slice; adjust only the weights to your risk profile.
Rule of thumb: 100 minus your age = percentage in stocks.

rules.title: Hypothesis-driven research pipeline
rules.rule: Start from a falsifiable hypothesis and follow a structured research pipeline; use coding tools only to speed testing.

sources.statement: Turn trading ideas into falsifiable hypotheses (market, event, information at decision time, horizon, competing explanation) before coding entries or committing capital.
Follow the institutional pipeline: define rules, get data, encode, backtest, analyze, optimize, check overfitting, automate, monitor.
Use AI coding to make ideas testable faster, not as a substitute for hypothesis formation, features and position management.

rules.title: Limit session time; stop after early trade
rules.rule: Limit discretionary trading to a short early window and stop for the day after the first trade or profit, because decision quality declines.

sources.statement: Switch an automated system off for the day once it has taken profit, even if its trading window is still open.
[Fabio Valentini] Decision quality declines after the first hour of scalping; limit discretionary scalping duration.
Trade gamma levels in the first 5-15 minutes of volatility, take the profit and stop for the day; extra trades after profits shift focus to money.
Stop trading for the day once a take profit is hit.
[Fredy Sarmiento] Decision quality deteriorates after the first trade; limit trading by time.

rules.title: Pre-map zones and wait
rules.rule: Mark zones in advance and trade only when price reaches a pre-mapped level.

sources.statement: Set price alerts at your planned levels, wait for them to trigger instead of chasing price, and confirm the setup still fits before executing.
Mark business zones from Market Profile in advance; you never know when price arrives, but you must be there when it does — no need to act otherwise.
Do not trade unless price is at a pre-mapped level; the market being open is not a reason to trade.
Bid in the most refined demand zone, and front-run large higher-timeframe demand zones with your bid.
Wait calmly for your setup like a sniper, then execute without hesitation.
Draw a normal volume profile, derive the business zone, and wait until price reaches it before looking closer.

rules.title: Psychology dominates trading success
rules.rule: Treat personality and inner psychology as major determinants of trading success.

sources.statement: Personality explains ~30% of a trader's fit; ~70% is inner resistance that must be identified and worked on.
Trading is psychology as much as technique; every trader thinks, feels and decides differently.
Talk about risk, not returns; personality decides over 80% of success.

rules.title: Size so total premium loss is acceptable
rules.rule: Size option positions on the maximum possible loss, so that losing the entire premium is tolerable.

sources.statement: Only buy an option if losing the entire premium fits your risk budget, and record strike, expiry and premium first.
Size trades on the maximum possible downside, not on targeted weekly/monthly premium.
Size a long option so that losing the entire premium would be acceptable; if you would not be okay with it going to zero, you are risking too much.
Before entering, ask whether you could handle the loss emotionally and financially; if not, do not take the trade.
Size debit spreads so going to zero is not the end of the world; if time remains and risk budget allows, buy back the short leg when the spread goes against you.

rules.title: Wait for consolidation after extended move
rules.rule: After an extended or overbought move, stand aside until consolidation forms a new setup.

sources.statement: Paid source: statement withheld.
After an extended trend, wait for consolidation before looking for a new entry signal.
Do not buy a breakout that is already extended with several legs up and far above VWAP.
Do not buy right after an exponential spike when RSI is overbought; wait for a dip or consolidation.
Do not chase news or geopolitical spikes; do due diligence first.
No new entry without consolidation first when a trend is advanced.
Avoid buying stocks that look overvalued after a big run; wait for a decline to buy good stocks at good prices.
After a vertical run-up and a vertical dump, expect no V-shaped recovery; wait for a base and consolidation before buying.

rules.title: Widening credit spreads warn of risk
rules.rule: Monitor high-yield credit spreads; widening is a leading recession and risk signal that warrants hedging or reducing risk.

sources.statement: Paid source: statement withheld.
When credit spreads widen while equities still rally, expect equities to follow credit and wait for credit to confirm before adding risk.
Widening credit spreads are a leading recession indicator; rising spreads mean the market perceives more economic risk.
Check credit (bond yields, CDS) alongside stocks; credit usually spots trouble before equities.
Check high-yield spreads and whether credit stress is spilling into equities before shorting or buying risk.
On a red stock day, check credit: if credit stays calm treat the drop as drama, if credit panics take it seriously.
Treat heavy insider selling plus distressed bond yields or record CDS costs on a company as warning signs.
Read high-yield spreads by level, direction and speed; treat a fast jump as a red light.

rules.title: Anti-martingale: scale up only with profits
rules.rule: Increase size only with profits or documented consistency, and remove added size when the edge weakens.

sources.statement: Use anti-martingale sizing: fixed ~0.25% base risk, add risk only with profits made while the model is working; stop after losses.
Remove added size when price returns toward breakeven or the edge weakens; increase live size only after documented consistency.
Increase account size and risk gradually in small steps instead of jumping to big size.
Do not increase risk per trade until you are profitable or at least break even.
Raise risk per trade only in steps as the account buffer grows, always keeping 10R in reserve.
Scale up size and accounts only after a few weeks to a month of consistent results at small size.

rules.title: Bond volatility speed hits equities
rules.rule: Watch the speed of bond volatility (MOVE, 10Y momentum), because rapid spikes drive equity declines.

sources.statement: Watch the speed of the 10-year move (MOVE index or momentum), not its level; rate of change matters more.
Check the MOVE index in a selloff: if the bond market is calm, the stress has not reached the foundation.
Watch MOVE-index/stock correlation: when high, rapid bond-volatility spikes translate into larger equity declines.

rules.title: Cap total options exposure
rules.rule: Cap total options exposure and short-premium collateral as a share of the portfolio.

sources.statement: Keep only about 10-20% of capital in options and do not commit more than about 80% of capital as collateral for short premium.
Keep LEAPS to about 10% of the portfolio and no more than 5% in any single LEAP.
Cap total options notional at about 75% of total portfolio value because a bad trade could undo years of building the portfolio.
Commit only part of the portfolio to the wheel, and skip it if the account is too small.

rules.title: Compare implied vs realized volatility
rules.rule: Judge option premium richness by comparing implied volatility with realized or historical volatility.

sources.statement: Your P&L is driven by realized volatility while price is set by implied; compare them rather than annualized premium yield.
Compare implied volatility to historical volatility to judge whether options are pricing in more fear than usual.

rules.title: Credit spread payoff mechanics
rules.rule: Treat a credit spread as a defined-risk trade where max profit is the net credit and max loss is the width minus the credit.

sources.statement: Credit spreads: max profit = net credit, max loss = width minus credit; nearer short strikes pay more credit but lower win probability.
A put credit spread sells one put and buys a lower put with the same expiration, collecting the net credit with capped (risk-defined) loss.

rules.title: Divergence needs confirmation
rules.rule: Use RSI or CVD divergence as an early warning only, never as a standalone trade.

sources.statement: Cumulative delta divergence (price up, CVD down) is useful but never trade it alone; always require confirmation.
Do not rely on RSI alone; it gives false signals, so use it mainly for divergence to confirm other analysis.
Use bearish RSI divergence (new price highs, falling RSI) as an advance warning, not confirmation.

rules.title: Don't chase beyond entry band
rules.rule: Enter close to the level and do not chase price beyond the defined entry band.

sources.statement: Paid source: statement withheld.
Enter near the level and do not chase; the closer to the level the smaller the risk.
Do not enter when price is stretched beyond the VWAP bands; it can retrace back to VWAP.

rules.title: Don't roll/repair broken spreads
rules.rule: Hold credit spreads to the profit or loss target and close broken ones rather than rolling or repairing them.

sources.statement: Do not try to repair a broken credit spread; if the thesis is broken by an unforeseen catalyst, rip off the band-aid and move on.
Hold credit spreads to the profit or loss target rather than rolling; enter and exit all legs together.

rules.title: Don't trade off moving averages
rules.rule: Do not use lagging indicators like moving averages as the reason for a trade.

sources.statement: Avoid lagging indicators and moving averages; the edge is entering when large players enter.
Learn moving averages and chart patterns because funds and algorithms use them, but do not make them the reason for a trade.

rules.title: Every edge has capacity limits
rules.rule: Evaluate an edge by how much capital it can absorb before slippage destroys it.

sources.statement: [Fabio Valentini] Evaluate an edge by its liquidity capacity, not only its technique; earnings-surprise edges have limited capacity.
Every model has a liquidity capacity; scalping models cannot absorb large capital without slippage destroying them.

rules.title: Favor relative strength leadership
rules.rule: Favor assets with price leadership versus the market, and treat relative weakness as a warning.

sources.statement: Paid source: statement withheld.
Relative weakness versus the market serves as a warning signal; be cautious.
Treat failed breakouts in leading stocks and sectors, including good news being sold, as a warning that the market may turn.
Rank assets by their past 12-month return excluding the most recent month, buy the top group (and short the bottom group for long-short), and rebalance monthly.
Among NQ, ES and YM, trade the index that is clearly weaker or stronger in your trade direction.

rules.title: Fit trading to your lifestyle
rules.rule: Pick strategies that fit your available time and trade around your life, not the reverse.

sources.statement: Trade around your life, not the reverse; simplify screens/subscriptions and move from day trading to selective swing trading.
Match strategy to available time: monthly covered calls/CSPs alongside long-term holdings fit limited time better than day trading.

rules.title: Focus on one concept
rules.rule: Master one simple concept at a time instead of mixing many methods.

sources.statement: Avoid style drift; stick to one approach, asset class and timeframe.
Stick with one simple concept, one level, one reaction, one pair to minimize variance; swing traders can use moving averages with wider stops.
Do not try to learn every team member's strategy at once; mixing scalping, swing and long-term methods made results worse.
Master one side (accumulation or distribution) before trading the other.
Become profitable in one market and master it before adding others.

rules.title: GEX is an estimate
rules.rule: Treat GEX levels as model-based proxies of dealer positioning, not observed facts or guarantees.

sources.statement: Aggregate dealer-gamma estimates rely on inventory assumptions; treat GEX as a proxy, not an observation of dealer positions.
GEX tools only estimate dealer positioning; treat levels as high-probability zones, never guarantees.

rules.title: Geopolitical risk premium decays
rules.rule: Fade geopolitical risk premium once headlines calm or the ceiling is known, and revert to the fundamentals-based position.

sources.statement: Paid source: statement withheld.
When balances are long, expect the market to revert to short/bearish positioning whenever geopolitical headlines calm down.

rules.title: High IV: use spreads to cut cost
rules.rule: When implied volatility is high, use debit spreads or sell put spreads instead of buying outright options.

sources.statement: If bullish but volatility is high, use a call spread or sell a put spread.
When implied volatility and premiums are high, use debit spreads to lower cost (capping gains); practice them first and keep them small.
Use spreads to cut cost, vega exposure and IV-crush risk compared with single long options.

rules.title: Honor stops, never widen them
rules.rule: Never move a stop further away, and always take the stop-out when wrong.

sources.statement: In a negative gamma selloff, let risk management take you out because the market can keep falling.
Never move the stop loss further away when a trade goes into drawdown or close winners immediately out of emotion.
[World Class Edge, speaker unattributed] Counter-trend trades run ~35-40% hit rate with 3:1-4:1 reward; you must stop out wrong-side positions every time.

rules.title: Index returns accrue overnight
rules.rule: Most index returns accrue overnight, so holding index longs from close to open captures the anomaly, especially after down days.

sources.statement: [Matteo Conti] Most index returns accrue overnight, not during regular hours; the overnight drift is expected to be stronger after down days and into the European open.
Overnight anomaly: most Nasdaq/S&P returns accrue from close to open; long at close, exit before open.

rules.title: Journal and review regularly
rules.rule: Keep a structured trading journal and review it regularly to improve.

sources.statement: Run a pre-trade, execution and post-trade cycle and keep a trading journal.
Keep a trading journal and review your logs to see what you did wrong and could improve.
Run daily pre-market analysis, keep a structured journal and hold weekly review sessions.
Give your full trade journal to an AI and ask for the number one emotional, psychological and mechanical cause of your losses.
Save a chart screenshot of every trade in your journal to review later.
Journal every trade: what you learned, the mechanical mistake, the emotional mistake behind it, and what your profitable self would tell you.
Count the losses that came from broken rules and what they cost: an AI review of his journal found over half his losses were rule breaks, costing $18,500 on his funded account.

rules.title: Keep an emergency fund
rules.rule: Hold 3-6 months of expenses in cash before investing the rest.

sources.statement: Keep three to six months of expenses in cash, separate from volatile positions, before taking market risk.
Hold an emergency fund covering 3-6 months of expenses before investing so you are never forced to sell investments prematurely.
Never hold more than 30% of net worth in cash; keep 3-6 months of expenses and invest the rest.
Keep an emergency fund, and pay down high-interest debt, before trading options or investing.
Pay off high-interest credit card debt and hold three to six months of expenses in cash before investing.
Keep an emergency reserve of at least about 5% of net worth in cash and invest the rest.

rules.title: Keep spread and condor wings narrow
rules.rule: Keep credit spread and condor wings narrow to limit tail losses.

sources.statement: When selling spreads keep them narrow, sell at least two weeks out, and compare the return to the ~5% risk-free yield.
Narrow condor wings (e.g., 100 to 50 wide) to cut tail losses; skew widths to the richer put side if warranted.

rules.title: Lower risk on personal than prop accounts
rules.rule: Take far less risk on personal accounts than in competitions or prop evaluations.

sources.statement: Competition risk is far higher than you should ever use on private or managed accounts.
When moving from prop accounts to your own cash, cut risk per trade sharply (he went from over $1,000 to $200-$300) for a month or two as a testing phase.
Personal accounts take far less risk than prop evaluations; do not risk 10% of a personal account.

rules.title: Macro, sentiment and price confluence
rules.rule: Enter only when macro/calendar, sentiment positioning and price action all point the same way.

sources.statement: Enter only when calendar/fundamental, sentiment (smart-money positioning) and trap/price-action perspectives point the same way; confluence gives ~80% conviction.
[Jan Smolen] Enter only when macro, fundamental calendar and sentiment perspectives point in the same direction.
Buy only when the macro backdrop, the business and the chart all line up; a great business with a broken chart is a bad entry.

rules.title: Never counter-trade at all-time highs
rules.rule: Never counter-trade at new all-time highs; fade only where old prices are accepted.

sources.statement: [World Class Edge, speaker unattributed] Never counter-trade at new all-time highs; counter-trade only at locations where old prices are being accepted and risk is defined.
Never counter-trade at new all-time highs; fade only at locations where old prices are being accepted.

rules.title: PbD push-range-breakout pattern
rules.rule: After a strong push and a range, enter on the exit from the range with a clear stop and target.

sources.statement: [Patrick Nill] PbD pattern: after a big push the market forms a range; enter on the exit from the range to follow the trend (or counter it).
Buy the breakout after a long, low-volume consolidation base rather than expecting V-shaped reversals.
P-pattern (push, then range): wait for price to leave the range and follow the trend (or counter it) with clear stop and target.

rules.title: RSI plus Bollinger overbought pullback
rules.rule: Expect a pullback only when overbought RSI combines with an upper Bollinger Band breach or rejection.

sources.statement: Do not sell on an overbought RSI alone; combine it with a Bollinger Band upper-band breach and close back inside to anticipate a pullback toward the middle band.
Paid source: statement withheld.

rules.title: Reduce size during losing streaks
rules.rule: Step down risk per trade, or the number of attempts, after repeated losses.

sources.statement: Reduce risk per trade during a losing streak.
After repeated failures, step down to smaller size, fewer attempts, or stop for the session.
After a string of losses, trade lighter to avoid emotional mistakes.

rules.title: Risk discipline framework essential
rules.rule: Build and consistently execute a risk framework that survives normal statistical variance.

sources.statement: [Imre Gams] Define the edge, then build a risk framework that survives normal statistical variance, and execute it with discipline repeatedly.
Without discipline and risk management you are dead regardless of capital.

rules.title: Robustness testing dominates the work
rules.rule: Spend most of your effort on developing and robustness-testing strategies rather than coding them or watching charts.

sources.statement: Coding is the least important part of a trading system; robustness testing takes most of the work.
Spend most of your time developing, testing and validating strategies, not watching charts.

rules.title: Roll short options for credit
rules.rule: Manage losing short puts or credit spreads by rolling, only for a net credit, or by buying back early for a small loss.

sources.statement: You need not hold a short put to expiration; if it goes against you, roll down/out or buy it back early to take a small loss and avoid a bigger one.
Roll a losing short put down and out only for a net credit; if no credit is available, accept assignment instead of paying a debit.
Roll losing credit spreads only for a net credit; rolling makes more sense for credit than debit spreads because time favors the seller.
Treat a credit spread that goes in the money as a losing trade: get out, or roll it out in time for a credit.

rules.title: S/R zones with role reversal
rules.rule: Treat support/resistance as zones where broken support becomes resistance.

sources.statement: Treat a predefined decision point as a zone, not an exact price.
Resistance forms where many people previously bought, because they sell when price returns; broken support becomes resistance.
Use support/resistance as zones, with role reversal (broken support becomes resistance); a zone is not automatically a trade.
In a downtrend, treat a retrace into a supply zone as the signal to exit longs or add to shorts.

rules.title: Sell the news on expected Fed cuts
rules.rule: Expect a possible sell-the-news reaction after a widely anticipated Fed cut, separating the decision from Powell's framing.

sources.statement: Expect possible sell-the-news after widely anticipated rate cuts; distinguish the FOMC decision from Powell's framing.
Expect sell-the-news behaviour around widely expected Fed cuts; keep sentiment neutral.

rules.title: Sentiment extreme plus catalyst reversal
rules.rule: Look for explosive reversals when one-sided sentiment meets an opposing catalyst.

sources.statement: Use the COT report for direction and wait for a catalyst to time the move.
Best setup: extremely one-sided bearish sentiment with bulls cornered, then a bullish catalyst arrives — expect an explosive, persistent reversal.
[Jan Smolen] Best setup: extreme one-sided sentiment (bulls obliterated, everyone short) followed by a bullish catalyst often produces an explosive reversal; get interested, then join early.
Buy into earnings only when the stock has already sold off and the fear is washed out, with defined conditions to see.

rules.title: Thesis needs technical confirmation
rules.rule: Require price confirmation, such as a resistance break or higher highs, before acting on a fundamental or macro thesis.

sources.statement: A favorable investment-clock phase still needs technical confirmation before entering.
Develop a thesis and enter only after price action confirms it instead of predicting.
Fundamentals alone are not enough; confirm price action has broken key resistance and is making higher highs before entering a LEAP.

rules.title: Think in probabilities, accept losses
rules.rule: Trade probabilities and accept individual losses as the cost of a consistent statistical edge.

sources.statement: Accept small losses as normal business when they fall within your strategy's statistics.
An edge is a statistical advantage applied consistently; accept individual losses like a casino.
Traders trade probabilities and risk.
Look for a small positive edge you can repeat many times, and size so you survive the swings along the way.
Forecast the distribution of outcomes, not a single price.

rules.title: Time stop on stalled thesis
rules.rule: Exit or roll if the setup or thesis has not triggered or played out within the planned time window.

sources.statement: Paid source: statement withheld.
If the thesis has not played out within a planned period, take a small loss or roll into a contract with more time.
If a trade does not start working within about four bars after entry, stop investing in it.
Exit slow-moving swing trades to redeploy the capital elsewhere.

rules.title: Vega/extrinsic rises with time and IV
rules.rule: Expect vega and extrinsic value to be largest ATM, longer-dated and at higher IV.

sources.statement: Vega is highest at the money and larger for longer-dated options.
Longer time to expiry and higher implied volatility raise option extrinsic value, which changes hedging pressure.

rules.title: Work limit orders near the mid
rules.rule: Work option limit orders near the bid-ask midpoint instead of paying the ask.

sources.statement: Work call spread limit orders just north of the mid to improve fills when bid/ask is wide.
Fish limit orders near the mark (bid-ask midpoint) instead of paying the ask.
Always use limit orders, never market orders, for multi-leg options spreads.
Always use limit orders for options, starting near the mid price, never market orders or the ask.

rules.title: Trade data surprise vs consensus
rules.rule: Trade the size of a data surprise versus consensus, conditioned on quantified thresholds, not the absolute value.

sources.statement: Set data triggers in advance: short bonds if inflation or wages print above the expected range, buy equities if inflation prints below it.
Big data surprises versus forecasts catch participants offside and often produce persistent moves; trade the surprise, not the level.
Treat widely expected events as already priced in.
What matters is the surprise versus consensus, not the absolute value of a release.
Expect equities to rally when CPI shows inflation falling, scaled to the size of the drop, and to fall if inflation rises.
Condition event trades on quantified surprises, e.g., long only if GDP beats by at least 0.6% at the defined support.
For USD after core PCE: a print at least 0.2% above expectations should favor the dollar.

rules.title: Covered call strike by expected view
rules.rule: Choose the covered-call strike by your view: OTM if you expect upside, ITM for downside protection when the stock is rich.

sources.statement: Strike covered calls by your view at expiration: OTM if you expect the stock to rise.
Sell a covered call only at a strike where you are comfortable letting the shares go; go far out of the money to keep them.
Mitigate covered-call negative asymmetry: choose strike by view (OTM for upside, ITM for protection) and sell fewer calls than shares owned.
If the stock is at all-time highs or rich, sell ITM covered calls for dollar-for-dollar downside protection to the strike.

rules.title: High market valuation means low returns
rules.rule: Treat elevated aggregate valuations (Rule of 20, ~21x P/E, Buffett Indicator) as expensive, with low forward returns.

sources.statement: Rule of 20: fair S&P 500 P/E ≈ 20 minus the inflation rate; above it stocks are expensive.
Use the Buffett Indicator (total US stock market value vs GDP) to judge overvaluation and hedge when extreme.
When the S&P 500 trades around 21x earnings, historical forward 5-year returns have been only ~3% per year.

rules.title: Investment clock regime
rules.rule: Classify regime by growth and inflation direction, pick assets accordingly, and act only when the clock and charts agree.

sources.statement: Identify whether growth and inflation are rising or falling and invest to fit that regime; stagflation favors gold and commodities.
Classify the regime with the investment clock (growth and inflation direction) and act only when clock and charts agree.
Use ISM above 50 and rising as a bullish business-cycle signal for stocks.
In a Goldilocks regime of falling inflation and holding or improving growth, favor stocks over bonds.
Falling growth and falling inflation (Reflation) favors bonds and defensive sectors such as staples, pharma and real estate.
Build the portfolio for the current economic environment and the next season, not last year's.
Rising growth with falling inflation (Recovery) favors stocks, especially communication services, discretionary and technology.
In stagflation, expect crowded growth leadership to crack and rotate toward inflation beneficiaries.

rules.title: Neutral between moving averages
rules.rule: Be bullish above both key moving averages and bearish below both, and stay neutral or scale out when price is between them.

sources.statement: Treat price between the 100- and 200-period MAs as a neutral, dangerous zone; scale out of positions as price approaches these averages and re-enter on a clear break.
Stay bullish when the market trades above both its 20- and 50-day SMAs; play the downside only after it breaks below both; be neutral in between.
Take a neutral stance when price is between the 20 and 50 SMAs or above one and below the other.

rules.title: Only trade planned edge setups
rules.rule: Take only planned trades where your edge is present and every checklist item is clear; skip impulse trades.

sources.statement: Before entering, verify the trade was planned; skip trades taken from boredom, hunches, or FOMO — like folding most poker hands.
Only take a scalp when you have a stock in play, a setup, a clear stop, and a trigger.
Once an alert system encodes your strategy, take trades only when an alert fires and take none when there is no alert.
Use a four-step checklist: trend, pattern, momentum confirmation, then timeframe/entry/stop/target; proceed only if each answer is clear.
Before every trade or add, ask whether it is a playbook trade, especially after a winner.
Use a written daily checklist of requirements that must all be met before you enter the market.
Trade only when your edge (recognizable chart patterns such as triangles, head-and-shoulders) is present; otherwise wait.

rules.title: Rate changes and differentials drive FX
rules.rule: Drive FX views from rate differentials and rate changes rather than absolute levels; cuts weigh on the currency.

sources.statement: Trade the currency of the strongest economy against the weakest, judged by growth, inflation and whether each central bank hikes or cuts.
For currencies, the interest-rate differential matters more than the absolute rate.
Trade FX on relative central bank pricing: the currency with more cuts priced weakens; judge the relative rate path, not one decision.
A rate cut usually weighs on that country's currency.
Focus on the change in rates, not the absolute level (e.g., Japan).

rules.title: Stress-test liquidity and correlation breaks
rules.rule: Stress-test for liquidity evaporation, basis blowouts and correlation breaks beyond what VaR assumes.

sources.statement: Complement VaR with stress tests: VaR assumes normal markets and stable correlations, and diversification benefits vanish when correlations break.
Do not rely on a stock-bond balance when both can fall at the same time; correlations break when you need them.
Focus risk work on basis blowouts, liquidity evaporation, operational delays and margin calls; desks die from these, not from wrong flat-price calls.
Expect correlations measured in calm times to rise in bear markets, which weakens diversification when it is needed.
Build worst-case exit scenarios that assume liquidity is gone; a plan that requires normal liquidity is not a scenario.

rules.title: Be patient with solid positions
